text: Bishop Copeland, Miss Foreman, and to all of the delegates attending this significant
conference of the Methodist Student Movement, ladies and gentlemen.
I need not pause to say how very delighted and honored I am to be here tonight and to
be a part of this very significant conference.
I certainly want to express my deep personal appreciation to the committee and to all of
you for extending the invitation.
It is always a rich and rewarding experience for me to take a brief break from the day-to-day
demands of our struggle for freedom and human dignity and discuss the issues involved in
that struggle with college and university students and concerned people of goodwill all
over this nation and all over the world.
So I can assure you that it is a great privilege to be here with you tonight and be grateful
to you for your warm expressions of support and I bring you greetings from those hundreds
and thousands of individuals who are involved in the civil rights struggle all over this
nation.
Many of you are involved in that struggle and we are all in it together and by and through
the grace of God and continued work we will be able to solve this great problem which
is the chief moral dilemma of our nation.
I'm sure that most of you have read that arresting little story from the pin of Washington
Irving entitled Rip Van Winkle.
And one thing that we usually remember about the story of Rip Van Winkle is that he slept
20 years.
But that is another point in that little story that is almost always completely overlooked.
It was a sign on the inn in the little town on the Hudson from which Rip went up into the
mountain for his long sleep.
When he went up the sign had a picture of King George III of England.
When he came down 20 years later the sign in the inn had a picture of George Washington.
The first president of the United States.
When Rip Van Winkle saw the picture of George Washington he was amazed.
He was completely lost.
He knew not who he was.
This tells us that the most striking thing about the story of Rip Van Winkle is not merely
that he slept 20 years but that he slept through a revolution.
While he was peacefully snoring up in the mountain, a great revolution was taken place
in the world, a revolution that at points would change the course of history.
And yet Rip knew nothing about it.
He was asleep.
That is nothing more tragic than to sleep through a revolution.
One of the great liabilities of history is that all too many people find themselves standing
amid a great period of social change.
And yet they fail to achieve the new attitudes, the new thought patterns, the new mental outlooks
that the new situation demands.
So many people fail to remain awake through great revolutions.
I need not remind you tonight that that is a great revolution taken place in our nation
and in the world.
It is a social revolution sweeping away an old order and bringing them to being a new order.
We have seen it on the international scale with the demise of colonialism and we see it
in our own nation with the gradual decline, the gradual defeat of the system of racial segregation.
The wind of change is blowing all over our world and all over our nation.
The great challenge facing everyone assemble here tonight, the great challenge facing America,
the great challenge facing every Christian is to remain awake through this great social revolution.
For we have basic Christian responsibilities and basic Christian challenges as a result of
this new age which is emerging.
And so tonight I would like to suggest some of the things that we must do if we are to be responsible
Christians and the midst of the racial revolution that is taken place in our nation and in the world.
First I'd like to say that we are challenged more than ever before to achieve a world perspective.
Any individual or any nation feels that it can live alone today is sleeping through a revolution.
But in a real sense we are all interdependent.
Not as true that the geographical oneness of our age has come into being to a large extent
because of man's scientific ingenuity.
Man through his scientific genius has been able to dwarf distance and place time in change.
Noget planes have compressed into minutes distances at once took weeks and even months.
I think Bob Hope has adequately described this new jet age in which we live.
And I know it isn't the usual thing for a Baptist preacher to be quoting Bob Hope.
But I think he's described this age very well.
He said it is an age in which it is possible to take a non-stop flight from Los Angeles
to New York City a distance of almost 3,000 miles.
And if on taking off in Los Angeles you develop hiccups, you will hick in Los Angeles and cup in New York City.
You know it is possible because of the time difference to take a flight from
Tokyo, Japan on Sunday night and arrive in Seattle, Washington on the preceding Saturday morning.
And when your friends ask you when you left Tokyo you will have to say I left tomorrow.
This is the kind of world in which we live. Now this is a bit humorous.
I'm trying to laugh a basic fact into all of us.
And it is simply this that man through his scientific genius and his technological genius
has made of this world a neighborhood.
Now we are challenged through our moral and ethical commitment to make over the brotherhood.
For we must all learn to live together as brothers or we will all perish together as foods.
This is a great challenge facing our nation and our world today.
No nation can live alone. No individual can live alone.
And it is necessary to see this.
I remember some time ago Mrs. King and I had the privilege of journeying to that great nation
known as India. I never will forget the experience.
It was a marvelous experience to meet and talk with the great leaders of India
and to meet and talk with hundreds and thousands of people all over the cities and villages of
that vast country. These experiences will remain dear to me as long as the courts of
memories are lengthened. But my friends, I say to you tonight that bear with those depressing moments.
How can one avoid being depressed when he sees evidences with his own eyes of millions of people
going to bed hungry at night? How can one avoid being depressed when he sees with his own eyes
millions of people sleeping on the sidewalks every night?
They have no beds to sleep in. They have no houses to go in.
How can one avoid being depressed when he discovers it out of India's population?
More than 400 million people, some 380 million make an income of less than $90 a year.
Most of these people have never seen a doctor or dentist.
As I notice these conditions, something within me cried out,
can we in America stand idly by and not be concerned in an answer came or no?
Because the destiny of the United States is tied up with the destiny of India and every other nation.
And I started thinking about the fact that we spend millions of dollars a day to store surplus food
in our country. I said to myself, I know where we can store that food free of charge,
in the wrinkles stomachs of the millions of God's children, in Asia,
in Africa, in South America, and in our own nation who go to bed hungry at night,
it may well be that we spend far too much of our national budget establishing military bases
around the world, rather than bases of genuine concern and understanding.
All I'm saying is simply this, that all life is interrelated.
And in a real sense, we are all caught in an inescapable network of mutuality tied in a single garment of
destiny. Whatever affects one directly affects all indirectly. For some strange reason,
I can never be what I ought to be until you are what you ought to be and you can never be what you
ought to be until I am what I ought to be. This is the interrelated structure of reality.
John Donne caught it years ago and placed it in graphic terms. No man is an island and tied
itself. Every man is a piece of the continent apart of the main. He goes on to the end to say,
any man's death diminishes me because I'm involved in mankind. Therefore never sinned to know for
whom the bail tolls. It tolls for thee. It seems to me that a recognition of this is a basic
responsibility that we as Christians face and the midst of the social changes that are taking place in
our world. Let me say secondly that we have a Christian responsibility in this racial crisis and
this revolution to reaffirm the essential immorality of racial segregation. Now over the last few years
we've had many important legal battles and all of these battles have been for the purpose of
establishing the constitutionality of integration and the unconstitutionality of segregation.
It was very important to have these legal battles. It was very important to have the supreme court
standing up in 1954 saying that separate facilities are inherently unequal and that the old
placid doctrine of 1896 must go. That to segregate a child on the basis of his race is to deny that child
equal protection of the law. This was important and remains important but where as Christians must come
to see not only the unconstitutionally constitutionality of segregation. We must reaffirm over and over
again that racial segregation is sinful and immoral whether it's in the public schools whether it's in
housing whether it is in the Christian church or any other area of life. Segregation is morally wrong
and sinful. Segregation is evil to use the words of the great Jewish philosopher Martin Bubba
because it substitutes an eye at relationship for the eye of our relationship. To use the thinking
of St. Thomas Aquinas segregation is evil because it is based on human laws that are out of harmony with
the moral natural and eternal laws of the universe. Somewhere the great theologian Paul Tillic has said
that sin is separation. What is segregation but an existential expression of man's tragic
estrangement is awful sinfulness is tragic separation and every Christian must see this and see that
segregation in any form is a cancer in the body politic of our nation which must be removed before
our democratic and moral health can be realized. We must set out to get rid of segregation all over
America now henceforth and forevermore this is a challenge facing every Christian.
Now the church has another thing that it can do in the ideational realm. It is necessary now
to get rid of the notion once and for all that they are superior and inferior.
The tragedy of segregation the tragedy of slavery is not only what it does to one in terms of physical
inconvenience but what it does to the soul these systems score the soul they damage the personality
they end up giving the segregator a false sense of superiority while leaving the segregated with
the false sense of inferiority. The whole doctrine of quite supremacy has been based on this idea
of one racial group being superior to another racial group. Now certainly many of the
scholars and in academic circles we have found individuals working in these areas and they've made it clear
that that is no evidence for this great anthropologist like Margaret Meade, Ruth Benedict,
the late Melvin Huskowitz and others made it clear that as a result of long years of study they see
no evidence for the idea of superior and inferior races that may be superior and inferior individuals
intellectually academically within all races but there are no superior or inferior races and yet
this notion still lingers around. Now there was a time strangely enough that men tried to justify
this notion on the basis of the Bible so tragic what people will do with religion and the Bible
to crystallize the status quo and rationalize and try to justify their own prejudices.
So the Bible and religion were misused to preserve an unjust status quo. It was argued that the Negro
was inferior by nature because of Noah's curse upon the children of Ham. Then the Apostle Paul's
Dictum became a watchword servants be obedient to your master and one brother had probably read
the logic of the great philosopher Aristotle. You will remember that Aristotle did a great deal to
bringing to being what we now know as pharmacological and then pharmacological there's a big word called
the syllogism. The syllogism has a major premise, a minor premise, and a conclusion. So this brother
decided to put his argument for the inferiority of the Negro and the framework of an Aristotelian
syllogism. He came out with his major premise. All men are made in the image of God. Then came his
minor premise. God as everybody knows is not a Negro. Therefore the Negro is not a man. This was a
kind of reasoning that prevailed. Now the whole I think people have gotten away from this. I hope so because
I read the other day where one of our white brothers in Mississippi said that God was a charter member
of the White Citizens Council but I think on the hold of people have gotten away from the biblical and
religious justification for. Now it's done on several sociological and cultural grounds.
You've heard the arguments. The Negro is not culturally ready for integration and if you integrate
of the schools and all areas of life you will pull the white race back a generation and then comes
the other argument. The Negro is a criminal. You see he has a large, a great crime rate and the
arguments going ahead in for 19. The individuals who said fourth these arguments never go on to say
if they are lagging standards in the Negro community and they're certainly all they lag because of
segregation and discrimination. Criminal responses are environmental and not racial. Social isolation,
economic deprivation, Z's, poverty breed, crime, whatever the racial group may be and it is a
torturous logic to use the tragic results of segregation as an argument for the continuation of it.
It is necessary to go back to the call to leave.
Somewhere we must come to see all over this land that all men are made in the image of God
and that that is no truth. The idea that that are superior and inferior racist we've had enough
examples of individuals who were members of oppress groups. Some are going amid the long night of
oppression and rising up to plunge against cloud field nights of affliction, new emblazing stars of
inspiration thereby justifying the conviction of the port. Fleecy locks and black complexion cannot
forfeit nature's claim. Skin may differ but affection dwells in black and white the same
where I so tall as to reach the pole or to grasp the ocean at a span. I must be measured by my soul.
The mind is a standard of the man and with this we can see the truth and the equality
of all mankind. Now after we've worked in these various areas of clearing up ideas
Christian responsibility means that it is necessary to engage in creative and massive action programs
to get rid of segregation and discrimination and our nation and racial injustice
wherever it exists in the world. In other words we must work not only in the realm of
developing a rather clearing up false ideas but it is necessary to work in the realm of action
in order to bring about the kind of reforms that would bring the changes that are necessary to make
racial justice a reality. Now as we're going to do this several things are necessary.
First it's the churches to move out into the arena of political action. I mean into the arena
of a massive action program it must remove the yoke of segregation from its own body.
This is a great challenge facing the Christian community all over this nation and I need not
to remind you my friends that in spite of the progress that has been made certainly some strides
have been made to make us all very happy. You've done things in the Methodist Church that are most
significant in this area and we're all inspired by. I just talked with my good friend Bishop
Thomas who has just been pointed to serve in an area where a Negro bishop has never served and most
of the congregations that fall under his jurisdiction happen to be white congregations. This happens
to be a marvelous step forward and it is always great to see the church moving on to remove the
shackles of segregation from its own body and in spite of the progress, in spite of the noble
pronouncements that have been made by so many ecclesiastical councils and so many of the conventions
and conferences of our great denominations within Protestantism and within Roman Catholicism.
We know that these pronouncements filter down all too slowly in some situations to local congregations
as I stand before you tonight. I must still say that the church is the most segregated
major institution in America and we must face the shameful fact. 11 o'clock on Sunday morning when
we stand to sing in Christ there is no east to west. We stand in the most segregated hour of America
the most segregated school of the week is the Sunday school. This means that all too many Christians
have had a high blood pressure of creeds and an anemones of these. Thank God we are beginning now to
shake the lethager from our souls and it is my hope that we will move on to get rid of segregation
in all of its dimensions within the church. That not only means the church itself the church institutions
such as hospitals such as colleges and universities and I must face the fact that my own home time
of Atlanta Georgia that I live right around the corner from the Georgia Baptist hospitals one of the
largest hospitals in Atlanta. But a Negro cannot be treated in that hospital. A Negro boy was hit
by an automobile not many months ago and carried to that hospital. A boy was all but dying and they
refused service. This is a hospital that has a name of the church. A big denomination indeed the
largest denomination in the south and so this means that that is a great deal of work that must be
done if we are to be true to the gospel of Jesus Christ and if we are to make it relevant in this
social situation. Now the other thing that the church must do is it removes a yoke of segregation from
its own body and an action program. It's got to get rid of one or two myths that make it impossible
to engage in action as long as you believe in. One is what I call the myth of time. I'm sure you've
heard this argument that only time can solve the problem of racial injustice. There are those who
still saying to the Negro and his allies and the white community just be nice and patient and
continue to pray and then a hundred or two hundred years of problem will work itself out because
only time can solve the problem. I believe that there's an answer to that myth and that is the time
is neutral. It can be used either constructively or destructively and I'm afraid my friends that the
forces of eel will in our nation, the extreme writers of our nation have used time much more
effectively than the forces of goodwill and it may well be that we will have to repent in this
generation not merely from the vitraulic words and the violent actions of the bad people who will
bomb a church in Birmingham, Alabama but for the appalling silence and indifference of the good
people who sit around and say wait on time somewhere along the way.
Somewhere we must come to see that human progress never rolls in on the wheels of inevitability.
It comes through the tireless efforts and the persistent work of dedicated individuals who are
willing to be co-workers with God and without this hard work time itself becomes an ally of the primitive
forces of social stagnation and so we must help time and we must realize that the time is always
right to do right. Now that is another myth that gets around a lot and I hope it will not influence
the church. It has influenced all too many segments of the church but I hope it will not do it any longer
that is the idea of that legislation can't really play a role in this period of social transition
because you got to change the heart. We heard that a great deal during the presidential campaign
and the pound of that with those who believed that and we heard Senator Goldwater repeat this over
the nation a great deal that legislation can't solve a problem and we face in civil rights and got
to change the heart and you can't change the heart through legislation. Now I would admit that at
least of those who follow that idea are uttering a half truth. I would agree that if this problem is
to be solved ultimately it will be necessary for men not merely to be obedient to that which can
be enforced by the law. They must rise to the majestic heights of being obedient to the unenforceable.
I realize that if this problem is to be solved ultimately it will be necessary for every
white person in this nation to delve down within to such as home, heart and soul come to see that
integration is what should be because it is natural and right and not merely because the law says it.
This problem is to be solved ultimately every white person of this country must treat every
Negro member of any minority group right because at bottom all men or brothers I realize this
and I must go on to give the other side because I am convinced of those who say that legislation can't
deal with this issue, happen to be uttering a half truth. It may be true that you cannot legislate
integration but you can legislate desegregation. It may be true that morality cannot be legislated
but behavior can be regulated. It may be true that the law can't change the heart but it can restrain
the heartless. It may be true that the law can't make a man love me but it can restrain him from
lynching me and I think that's pretty important also.
So while the law may not be able to change the hearts of men it does change the habits of men
and when you begin to change the habits of men pretty soon the attitude will be changed and the
hearts will be changed. So it is a role of the Church to support meaning for legislation
and I'm happy to say that as we were struggling to get the civil rights bill through
and we had the support of so many elements and segments of the Church community all across this
nation and I'm convinced that the civil rights bill is a reality today because the religious forces
of our nation are willing to join with the civil rights organizations and the other forces of good
will and it was this coalition of conscience that brought it about and this kind of coalition of
conscience must continue if our problems ought to be solved. We have a problem now in many states
no state really can boast of clean hands in the area of brotherhood but we know that some are
worse than others and that is a state in our union which I believe everybody here tonight is concerned
about even those who may live in that state because one cannot love a situation bless somehow in
the midst of that love in love they seek to rectify the situation I live in the south
and I say to you I love the south and I'm going to stay there and work with this problem in my love for the south.
And I think it is time for all people of good will in this country including the people of good will who
live in the state of Mississippi to rise up now and say Mississippi cannot continue to trample over its
Negro citizens with our feet of oppression that almost that almost a million Negroes living in
Mississippi some nine hundred and seventy thousand to be exact almost four hundred and seventy five thousand
heart of voting age and yet only at about twenty eight thousand registered last year
state of Mississippi only allowed sixteen hundred and some Negroes to register she continues at this
pace it will take exactly one hundred and thirty two years to get half of the eligible Negroes in the
state of Mississippi registered this cannot continue something must be done to arouse a conscience of the
state of Mississippi something must be done to cause persons within that state to rise up
but no state in our union has more blatantly trampled over the basic human rights of its citizens
and the state of Mississippi no state in our union has brutalized and terrorized its citizens as much
as a state of Mississippi no state has murdered as many individuals without having anything done
about it and now something must be done that is a challenge getting ready to take place next Monday
there's a challenge that should concern everybody of goodwill that challenge will be
the basis of the fact that the congressman of that state are improperly elected because of the
whole cell denied the right to vote to the Negro citizens of the state of Mississippi and there

and let him know that you want him to vote in favor of the challenge so that these congressmen

have to stand up
if our House of Representatives will go on record seating these five congressmen
it will only give encouragement to the brutality to the violence and to man's and humanity to man

because this is so basic after we have cleared up the mists that surround us and support it legislation
it is necessary for the church to support the action programs which move out into the arena of

in their struggle for freedom and human dignity I am still convinced that if the Negroes

nobody within a sense loves to go to jail if he puts you in jail you go in that jail and transform it

he had been fit to live this is what the nonviolence is
so that is power in this way because it has a way of disarming the opponent but not only this it gives
